title: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it in place and return the new head. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
keyPoints: Three pointers: previous (starts null), current (starts at head), and a saved next for the forward link.
At each step: save next, reverse the link (current.next = previous), then advance both pointers.
When current becomes null, previous is the new head of the reversed list.
Saving next before overwriting current.next is mandatory or you lose the rest of the list.
Time is O(N) and space is O(1): no new nodes allocated, no recursion stack used.
The same three-pointer skeleton underlies sublist reversal, k-group reversal, and rotation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep previous, current, and a saved next; point current back to previous each step, and previous ends as the new head.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **In-place reversal** walks the list once, redirecting each node's `next` pointer to the previous node.
- Three references: `previous` (initially null), `current` (initially head), and a **saved `next`**.
- At each node: `next = current.next`, `current.next = previous`, `previous = current`, `current = next`.
- When `current` becomes null, `previous` is the **new head**.
- **No new nodes** allocated, so space is O(1).
- This skeleton powers **sublist reversal, k-group reversal, and rotation**.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction slips are stored as a singly linked chain in oldest-first insertion order. To display them newest-first for a customer statement, a clerk unclips each slip and re-clips it to the slip that came before, moving down the chain once. At the end, the last slip is the new front of the chain.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a singly linked list in place is the foundation of the entire in-place reversal pattern. It rests on three pointers: previous (trailing behind), current (being processed), and a saved next (preserving the forward link before it is overwritten). At each node, you save next, reverse the link by pointing current back to previous, then slide both pointers forward. When current falls off the end, previous is the new head.

The saved next pointer is not optional. The instant you reassign current.next to previous, you destroy the only forward reference to the rest of the list. Without saving it first, the remaining nodes are lost. This runs in O(N) time and O(1) space, and the iterative version is preferred over recursion for production because recursion would consume O(N) stack space on long lists.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to render transaction statements newest-first. Transaction slips were stored as a singly linked chain in oldest-first insertion order, and the chains could be very long. The three-pointer in-place reversal flipped each chain in a single pass with no extra allocation, which was critical for memory-constrained batch processing.

The senior-level insight is that this same three-pointer skeleton, with different start and stop conditions, powers sublist reversal, k-group reversal, and rotation. Mastering the base case means all the variants follow naturally.

Remember one sentence: save next, reverse the link, advance both pointers, and previous ends as the new head.
